title: India's Retail Investors Just Absorbed the Biggest Foreign Selloff in History — and JP Morgan Says They Won't Stop
excerpt: Foreign portfolio investors have pulled over ₹2.67 lakh crore from Indian equities in 2026 — but monthly SIP inflows above ₹30,000 crore have made the market almost self-sustaining.
body:
Foreign portfolio investors have been pulling money out of Indian equities at a pace never seen before. Over ₹2.67 lakh crore (roughly $28 billion) has left the market in 2026 alone — surpassing the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn during the entirety of 2025, according to National Securities Depository data.

In any previous era, an outflow of this magnitude would have triggered a full-blown market crisis. Yet the Nifty 50 just posted its third consecutive weekly gain, and the Sensex is holding comfortably above 77,000.

The reason is structural, not sentimental. India's domestic retail investors — channelling money through Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) with the discipline of a monthly utility payment — have become the market's primary load-bearing wall. And according to a new equity strategy report from JP Morgan, they are not going anywhere.

## The Numbers That Changed Everything

India's mutual fund industry recorded its 63rd consecutive month of positive equity inflows in May 2026 — a streak that began in March 2021 and has survived a pandemic recovery, a global rate-hike cycle, a war in West Asia, and now the largest FPI exodus in Indian market history.

SIP contributions stood at ₹30,953 crore in May, up nearly 16% year-on-year. The number of contributing SIP accounts reached 9.64 crore — nearly 100 million individual recurring investment mandates, each one automatically debiting a bank account on a fixed date every month.

SIP assets now represent roughly 21% of the entire mutual fund industry's assets under management, which crossed ₹80 lakh crore earlier this year. This is no longer a niche behaviour — it is a structural feature of how Indian households save.

## What JP Morgan Is Saying

JP Morgan's report attributes the resilience of domestic inflows to two reinforcing forces: **tax policy and habit formation**.

India's 12.5% long-term capital gains tax on equities — introduced in 2024's budget alongside the removal of indexation benefits for other asset classes — has tilted the relative attractiveness of equities sharply upward. For salaried professionals in the 30% bracket, equities now offer the most tax-efficient route to wealth accumulation. Real estate, fixed deposits, and gold all carry higher effective tax rates after the indexation change.

"The inflows should continue due to tax and policy," JP Morgan wrote in its report. The bank projects sustained equity inflows through FY2026 and FY2027, underpinned by what it calls a "structural migration of Indian household savings into financial assets."

This is not speculative. In April 2026, when FPIs pulled out ₹60,847 crore from Indian equities, domestic institutional investors — led by mutual funds — bought ₹51,064 crore. The net gap was modest, and the market rallied 10% that month. In May, the same pattern held: FPI outflows were absorbed by DII inflows, and the market moved sideways rather than down.

## Why Foreign Investors Are Leaving — and Why It Matters Less Than It Used To

The FPI exodus is driven by a specific global narrative. Capital is rotating toward AI and semiconductor plays — KOSPI surged over 200% in the past year on the back of Korean and Taiwanese chip stocks, while India's IT index has fallen by more than a third since late 2024. SpaceX's anticipated IPO, Nvidia's continued run, and the broader AI infrastructure buildout are pulling liquidity toward technology-heavy markets.

India's listed universe, worth roughly $5 trillion, is concentrated in banks, energy, consumption, and industrial conglomerates. It has no AI or semiconductor champion of comparable scale. As Ambit Capital bluntly noted in a June 22 strategy note: "Capital is moving to where the next growth cycle lives."

But the structural takeaway for NRI investors is that this rotation, while real, no longer dictates India's market direction. Domestic flows are now large enough — and sticky enough — to absorb FPI selling without structural damage. This is a fundamentally different market from 2013, when the "taper tantrum" triggered a 20% Nifty decline, or even from 2018, when FPI outflows were measured in the thousands of crores and felt consequential.

## What NRIs Should Watch

The SIP phenomenon has direct implications for NRI investors thinking about India allocations:

**Market floor is higher.** The SIP conveyor belt creates persistent buying pressure that cushions corrections. Sharp drawdowns are shorter and shallower than they would be in a FPI-dominated market. The Nifty's recovery from its March 2026 lows — when it fell 14.5% — took weeks, not months.

**Valuations are structurally supported.** MSCI India trades at 24 times earnings, below its five-year average of 25.8 times. While this remains a premium to the broader MSCI Emerging Markets index (18.8x), the domestic buying floor makes mean-reversion to deep discount levels unlikely unless SIP flows themselves break down — which JP Morgan's analysis suggests is improbable in the near term.

**Bond market is opening up.** Separately, Goldman Sachs recommended going long India's 30-year government bonds this week, citing the RBI's recent capital flow measures, easing inflation, and the likely inclusion of Indian bonds in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index. FPI debt flows in June hit a 15-month high of $4.2 billion, boosted by the government's June 5 decision to exempt capital gains and interest tax on foreign investments in government securities.

**The AI gap is real but addressable.** India's corporate sector does not yet have the innovation-driven cash flows to compete in the AI era, but infrastructure plays — data centres, power generation, semiconductor fabs under construction — are emerging as indirect beneficiaries. The ₹76,000-crore semiconductor PLI scheme is beginning to attract real investment, and the Tata-PSMC fab in Gujarat is on track for first output in 2027.

For NRIs weighing whether to add to India exposure or pull back in line with FPI sentiment, the data suggests that India's market is increasingly a domestic story. The risks remain — global recession, oil shocks, a breakdown in SIP discipline — but the structural resilience that SIPs have built is unlike anything Indian markets have had before.

As the IndMoney research note from April put it: "FIIs sold. DIIs bought. The market still went up. That framework of reading FII data as the main directional signal for the Indian market is dated."

*Based on data from NSDL, AMFI, JP Morgan Equity Strategy, Goldman Sachs Economics Research, Morningstar Offshore Fund Spy, and Outlook Business.*
